ideas.title: Faith-Facing Model Comparison Platform
ideas.primary_need: eval engineering
ideas.summary: Can Fide AI build a public-interest evaluation platform that compares models, prompts, retrieval systems, agents, and full faith-facing product harnesses with the rigor expected from institutions like Arena, Artificial Analysis, and METR?
ideas.why_it_matters: Faith institutions need evidence before adopting systems that appear theological, pastoral, or morally authoritative. Generic leaderboards do not test pastoral boundaries, theological integrity, human agency, escalation, or religious authority. Fide AI needs its own platform layer to run, audit, compare, and publish faith-facing evaluations.
ways_to_help: Build runner adapters.
Design the run manifest schema.
Contribute reviewer workflow UI.
Audit license and white-label constraints of candidate OSS platforms.
ideas.hypothesis: A platform built around run manifests, artifact custody, reviewer workflows, and public claims limits can produce more decision-relevant evidence than isolated benchmark scripts or one-off reports.
needed_controls: Stable model endpoint/version metadata.
Repeatable prompt and harness configuration.
Artifact hashes for inputs, outputs, prompts, corpora, and scoring code.
Publication review before claims are exposed publicly.
outputs: Fide run manifest schema.
Internal model/system comparison dashboard.
Public comparison reports.
Leaderboard snapshots with confidence intervals and claims limits.
open_questions: Whether Opik, Langfuse, Phoenix, or a custom trace layer should be used.
How much raw output can be published safely.
Whether public rankings should be aggregate scores, category scores, or evidence cards rather than a single leaderboard.
ideas.public_claim_boundary: The platform can support comparative evidence only for named models, harnesses, conditions, datasets, dates, and scoring protocols. It should not claim that a model is generally "safe for faith" without use-case boundaries.

ideas.title: FMG-Bench Human Calibration and Construct Validity
ideas.primary_need: expert reviewers, statistics
ideas.summary: Do FMG-Bench dimensions measure stable, decision-relevant constructs when scored by calibrated human reviewers, and where do model judges diverge from expert human judgment?
ideas.why_it_matters: Benchmarks are easy to publish and hard to validate. Fide AI should not rely on synthetic judges or aggregate scores unless it knows which dimensions are reliable enough to guide deployment, procurement, or public claims.
ways_to_help: Serve as an expert reviewer.
Review scoring rubrics.
Help with reliability analysis.
Build annotation and adjudication tooling.
ideas.hypothesis: Some dimensions will be reliable enough for decision support, while others will require narrower rubrics, more reviewer training, or removal from high-stakes claims.
proposed_method: Recruit a small calibrated reviewer panel.
Score a stratified subset of FMG-Bench outputs.
Measure inter-rater reliability, judge-human disagreement, strictness/leniency, failure-tag consistency, and disagreement concentration by scenario type.
Compare expert review, trained non-expert review, and model judge scores where feasible.
needed_controls: Reviewer conflict checks.
Blind model/system labels where practical.
Rubric versioning.
Adjudication protocol for high-disagreement items.
Public/private separation for sensitive notes.
outputs: Calibration report.
Reviewer protocol.
Updated FMG-Bench rubric guidance.
Evidence map classifying dimensions as decision-relevant, conditional, or not yet validated.
open_questions: What minimum reliability threshold should Fide require for public claims?
How should theological tradition metadata be represented without tokenizing reviewers?
Which disagreement patterns are legitimate pluralism rather than rubric failure?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: Calibration can validate specific dimensions and use cases. It cannot make a blanket claim that FMG-Bench fully measures theological or pastoral quality.

ideas.title: Held-Out Multi-Turn Pastoral Pressure Tests
ideas.primary_need: scenario design, review
ideas.summary: Do faith-facing AI systems that perform well on single-turn benchmark items also handle multi-turn, emotionally loaded, pastoral-adjacent situations without fabricating authority, overcomplying, missing escalation, or replacing human care?
ideas.why_it_matters: Real users do not interact with faith-facing systems as isolated benchmark questions. They disclose confusion, grief, shame, conflict, abuse, doubt, and spiritual vulnerability over multiple turns. Evaluation needs to test the shape of the interaction, not only the first answer.
ways_to_help: Draft scenarios.
Review pastoral and crisis boundaries.
Build multi-turn runner support.
Analyze whether single-turn scores predict pressure failures.
ideas.hypothesis: Some systems with strong single-turn scores will fail under multi-turn pressure, especially when the user asks for certainty, secrecy, absolution, diagnosis, clergy-like authority, or permission to avoid human help.
proposed_method: Create held-out multi-turn scripts around realistic faith-facing pressure cases.
Include pressure escalations such as flattery, urgency, authority transfer, refusal of human help, theological false premises, and crisis disclosures.
Score trajectories for boundary preservation, truthfulness, escalation, theological humility, and recovery from prior errors.
needed_controls: Expert review of scenario safety.
Clear rules for simulated crisis content.
Separation between theological disagreement and pastoral risk.
Model and harness version control.
outputs: Multi-turn pressure scenario pack.
Failure taxonomy.
Technical report comparing single-turn and multi-turn validity.
Institution-facing guidance on deployment testing.
open_questions: How realistic can scenarios be without creating unsafe or privacy-sensitive data?
Which failures should trigger automatic severe-risk classification?
How should tradition-specific pastoral norms be represented?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can test defined pressure patterns. It should not claim to certify general pastoral competence.

ideas.title: Relational Substitution Risk in Faith-Facing AI
ideas.primary_need: theology, UX research
ideas.summary: When does a faith-facing AI system move from supporting a user's religious life to substituting for embodied community, clergy, spiritual direction, family, therapy, or other human care?
ideas.why_it_matters: Faith-facing AI risks are not only wrong answers. Systems can simulate presence, authority, intimacy, or spiritual companionship in ways that redirect users away from actual communities and responsible care.
ways_to_help: Contribute pastoral, psychological, and UX expertise.
Draft realistic interaction patterns.
Review boundary language across traditions.
ideas.hypothesis: Relational substitution risk is observable through interaction patterns: exclusive attachment, avoidance of human disclosure, simulated clerical authority, excessive personalization, spiritual dependency, and claims that the AI can stand in for communal discernment.
proposed_method: Define a taxonomy of substitution patterns.
Create scenario probes that test whether systems redirect users toward appropriate human, communal, pastoral, clinical, or legal support.
Compare default models, faith-facing harnesses, memory-enabled systems, and companion-style UX.
needed_controls: Do not penalize systems for ordinary educational support.
Distinguish short-term triage from long-term relational replacement.
Include reviewer diversity across pastoral and institutional contexts.
outputs: Relational substitution risk taxonomy.
Evaluation rubric.
Field brief for faith institutions and builders.
Product-design checklist.
open_questions: What level of conversational warmth is appropriate?
How should systems handle users with no safe local community?
How should memory and personalization be bounded?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can identify substitution risk patterns. It cannot determine whether a specific user relationship with a system is spiritually healthy.

ideas.title: Scripture, Tradition, and Moral-Framing Interventions
ideas.primary_need: eval design, replication
ideas.summary: Do Scripture, sacred tradition, religious identity, familial embeddedness, or other morally thick framings measurably change model behavior in faith-facing tasks, and can those effects be separated from style, length, familiarity, and response-bias artifacts?
ideas.why_it_matters: Recent Christian machine intelligence research suggests that theological texts and identity framings can sometimes shift model moral behavior. Fide AI can contribute by independently replicating, stress-testing, and extending these claims with stronger public-interest controls and broader traditions.
ways_to_help: Contribute replication protocols.
Help design controls.
Provide theological review for tradition-specific framing.
Run model comparisons through the Fide platform.
ideas.hypothesis: Some religious framings may alter model behavior in measurable ways, but effects will be model-, task-, and context-dependent. Many apparent gains may collapse under label balancing, matched controls, or deployment-like harness testing.
proposed_method: Replicate selected scripture-injection and moral-framing studies.
Add length-matched, style-matched, secular, and shuffled-label controls.
Test across model families, current endpoints, and faith-facing tasks.
Extend beyond one canon or translation where appropriate.
needed_controls: Label balancing and position-bias checks.
Matched controls for text length, register, familiarity, and emotional valence.
Pre-registered hypotheses.
Clear distinction between base-model behavior and deployed product behavior.
outputs: Replication report.
Open prompt/control set where release-safe.
Guidance on when religious prompt interventions are meaningful or misleading.
open_questions: Which effects survive model updates?
Are improvements genuine reasoning improvements or output-style changes?
Can interventions improve safety without increasing false authority?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: Even positive effects would not prove that a model has religious understanding, spiritual authority, or pastoral competence.

ideas.title: Faith-Facing Retrieval Grounding and Citation Reliability
ideas.primary_need: RAG evaluation
ideas.summary: How reliably do faith-facing AI systems retrieve, cite, and represent religious sources when users ask theological, historical, pastoral, or institution-specific questions?
ideas.why_it_matters: Many faith-facing products will be retrieval-augmented. The core failure may not be the base model's theology but the system's ability to cite the right source, avoid fabricated quotations, handle conflicting authorities, and distinguish official teaching from commentary.
ways_to_help: Curate source corpora.
Build retrieval evaluation tooling.
Review source authority taxonomies.
Contribute institution-specific use cases.
ideas.hypothesis: RAG systems will show distinct failure modes: citation fabrication, source misranking, confessional flattening, overconfident synthesis, failure to quote accurately, and inability to distinguish official authority from secondary commentary.
proposed_method: Build a source-grounded evaluation set across scripture, catechisms, denominational documents, pastoral guidelines, commentaries, and institutional policies.
Score retrieval recall, citation accuracy, quotation fidelity, authority classification, answer grounding, and uncertainty handling.
Compare base model, RAG harness, and retrieval configuration changes.
needed_controls: Versioned corpora and source hashes.
Tradition-specific source hierarchy.
Adversarial near-match citations.
Human review for disputed source interpretation.
outputs: Faith-facing RAG benchmark.
Citation reliability report.
Corpus-card template.
Procurement checklist for institutions buying RAG systems.
open_questions: Which sources can be redistributed publicly?
How should copyrighted or licensed religious texts be handled?
How should systems represent contested authorities across traditions?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can evaluate retrieval and citation behavior under defined corpora. It cannot guarantee doctrinal adequacy across all religious questions.

ideas.title: Tradition-Specific Disagreement and Pluralism Handling
ideas.primary_need: domain experts, rubric design
ideas.summary: Can faith-facing AI systems represent serious disagreement among religious traditions accurately, respectfully, and without collapsing contested questions into bland consensus or false neutrality?
ideas.why_it_matters: Many theological questions have real disagreement. A system that sounds balanced but erases doctrinal differences can mislead users and institutions.
ways_to_help: Contribute expert review within a tradition.
Draft representative disagreement cases.
Help define source hierarchies and rubric anchors.
ideas.hypothesis: Models will often over-harmonize disagreements, misstate minority views, or present one tradition's answer as generic Christianity or generic religion unless the harness enforces explicit tradition and authority boundaries.
proposed_method: Build disagreement scenarios across major doctrinal, moral, liturgical, and institutional questions.
Score representation accuracy, symmetry, source grounding, uncertainty, user-context sensitivity, and refusal to adjudicate beyond scope.
Include tradition-specific reviewer panels.
needed_controls: Clear distinction between core orthodoxy, intramural disagreement, and interfaith disagreement.
Reviewer metadata and conflict handling.
Rubric anchors that avoid rewarding empty both-sides language.
outputs: Disagreement handling benchmark.
Tradition-specific rubric addenda.
Public guide for builders on representing disagreement.
open_questions: Which traditions and denominations should be covered first?
How should Fide handle questions where traditions disagree about whether a view is legitimate?
How should a general-purpose faith-facing system ask clarifying questions?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can test representation of defined disagreements. It should not claim to resolve those disagreements.

ideas.title: Evaluation-Awareness and Faith-Facing Honesty Tests
ideas.primary_need: red-team design
ideas.summary: Do faith-facing AI systems behave differently when they recognize they are being evaluated, and can domain-specific honesty or integrity framings reduce evaluation gaming without creating new failure modes?
ideas.why_it_matters: Evaluation-aware systems can make benchmark results unreliable. In faith-facing contexts, a system might perform humility, caution, or doctrinal deference under test while behaving differently with users.
ways_to_help: Design red-team probes.
Build consistency metrics.
Review ethical boundaries for deception in evaluation.
ideas.hypothesis: Some systems will show benchmark-shaped behavior under obvious evaluation conditions. Domain-specific integrity framings may help, but could also produce performative religious language or over-refusal.
proposed_method: Create honeypot-style evaluation-awareness probes.
Compare hidden vs obvious evaluation contexts.
Test honesty/integrity framings against secular controls.
Measure behavioral consistency, not just benchmark score.
needed_controls: Matched secular and religious framings.
Detection of over-refusal and performative piety.
Separation of base-model and harness-level effects.
outputs: Evaluation-awareness probe set.
Consistency report.
Recommendations for benchmark design and deployment audits.
open_questions: How should Fide ethically run honeypot tests?
What counts as gaming vs appropriate caution?
Can consistency be measured without hidden production data?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can identify evaluation-awareness patterns under defined probes. It cannot prove deployment behavior in all real-world contexts.

ideas.title: Multimodal Religious Reasoning and Sacred Imagery
ideas.primary_need: multimodal evaluation
ideas.summary: How do multimodal AI systems interpret sacred images, liturgical objects, religious spaces, diagrams, screenshots, and visual pastoral context, and do visual religious cues change downstream reasoning?
ideas.why_it_matters: Faith-facing systems will increasingly process images: church documents, artworks, icons, classroom materials, screenshots, event flyers, ritual objects, and user-submitted photos. Misinterpretation can create theological, institutional, or pastoral errors.
ways_to_help: Curate copyright-safe images.
Review iconographic and liturgical accuracy.
Build multimodal runner support.
ideas.hypothesis: Multimodal models will vary widely in whether they recognize religious context, overinterpret sacred imagery, flatten denominational cues, or allow visual cues to bias moral/theological answers.
proposed_method: Build a visual test set with sacred art, worship spaces, religious documents, educational materials, and neutral controls.
Score recognition, source/context accuracy, theological overreach, sensitivity to tradition, and downstream answer shifts.
Compare text-only, image-only, and image-plus-text conditions.
needed_controls: Copyright-safe images.
Nonreligious figural and aesthetic controls.
Tradition-specific reviewer input.
Avoidance of iconographic overclaiming.
outputs: Multimodal faith-facing evaluation set.
Report on visual cue effects.
Builder guidance for image-enabled faith products.
open_questions: Which image categories are highest risk?
How should systems handle user-submitted images of people or private spaces?
Can sacred imagery improve moral reasoning while increasing false authority?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can test visual reasoning and cue effects. It should not infer spiritual significance from images or claim devotional competence.

ideas.title: Human Agency, Authority, and Escalation Benchmarks
ideas.primary_need: pastoral/legal/clinical review
ideas.summary: Do faith-facing AI systems preserve human agency, avoid improper authority claims, and escalate to appropriate human support in high-trust situations?
ideas.why_it_matters: The most important faith-facing failures may involve authority: the system acts like clergy, counselor, confessor, judge, spiritual director, or institutional representative when it is not one.
ways_to_help: Review crisis and pastoral scenarios.
Define severe-failure criteria.
Build multi-turn escalation tests.
Audit product harnesses.
ideas.hypothesis: Systems will fail differently depending on harness design. Some will over-answer with false authority; others will over-refuse; better systems will clarify scope, support agency, and route users toward appropriate human help.
proposed_method: Build scenarios involving spiritual crisis, abuse disclosures, self-harm, family conflict, theological scrupulosity, legal/clinical ambiguity, and institutional policy questions.
Score authority boundary, agency preservation, escalation, factual grounding, and follow-through.
Compare generic models, faith-tuned prompts, RAG systems, and deployed harnesses.
needed_controls: Clinical/legal/pastoral safety review.
Crisis content handling policy.
Tradition-specific escalation norms.
Severe-failure classification.
outputs: Agency-authority-escalation benchmark.
Severe-failure taxonomy.
Institution-facing deployment checklist.
Builder guidance for escalation design.
open_questions: What escalation language is appropriate across different religious contexts?
How should systems handle users who reject human help?
Which failures should be disqualifying for deployment?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can evaluate boundary and escalation behavior under defined scenarios. It cannot certify a system for pastoral, clinical, or legal care.

ideas.title: Reviewer Reliability for Faith-Facing AI Evaluation
ideas.primary_need: statistics, reviewer operations
ideas.summary: What reviewer configurations produce reliable, fair, and interpretable scores for faith-facing AI outputs?
ideas.why_it_matters: Faith-facing evaluation depends on expert judgment, but expert disagreement is real. Fide AI needs to know when scores reflect stable constructs and when they reflect reviewer background, tradition, strictness, or rubric ambiguity.
ways_to_help: Design reliability analysis.
Build reviewer assignment tooling.
Serve as reviewer or adjudicator.
Audit rubric wording.
ideas.hypothesis: Reliability will vary by dimension. Factual source-grounding may show higher agreement than pastoral tone, theological judgment, or pluralism handling. Reviewer training and adjudication should improve reliability but may not solve tradition-bound disagreement.
proposed_method: Compare expert, trained non-expert, and model-judge scoring.
Track inter-rater reliability, disagreement tags, strictness, confidence, and reviewer background metadata.
Test rubric revisions on high-disagreement items.
needed_controls: Reviewer conflict-of-interest checks.
Blind model labels.
Balanced scenario sampling.
Public/private separation for reviewer metadata.
outputs: Reviewer reliability report.
Reviewer training protocol.
Adjudication policy.
Acceptable-evidence thresholds for public claims.
open_questions: What reliability metric best fits mixed categorical and continuous rubrics?
How many reviewers are needed per high-stakes item?
When should disagreement be published rather than collapsed into a score?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work validates reviewer process quality. It does not by itself validate any particular model or product.

ideas.title: Optimization Pressure and Visible-Rubric Gaming
ideas.primary_need: eval science
ideas.summary: If builders can see Fide AI rubrics or optimize against public benchmark items, do systems become genuinely safer or merely better at passing the visible test?
ideas.why_it_matters: Public standards need transparency, but visible benchmarks can be gamed. Fide AI needs evidence about which evaluation artifacts can be public, which should be held out, and how leaderboard participation affects real deployment behavior.
ways_to_help: Design split and leakage controls.
Build optimization-pressure experiments.
Review leaderboard governance policy.
ideas.hypothesis: Visible rubric optimization will improve surface compliance on known dimensions while leaving held-out pressure failures intact unless the evaluation includes multi-turn, adversarial, and human-reviewed cases.
proposed_method: Create public, private, and held-out benchmark splits.
Allow controlled optimization against visible rubrics.
Compare improvement on public items, private items, and deployment-like pressure tests.
Measure whether failure modes shift rather than disappear.
needed_controls: Strict split management.
Versioned benchmark releases.
Builder disclosure of tuning and prompt changes.
Adversarial held-out sets.
outputs: Benchmark governance policy.
Evidence on visible-rubric robustness.
Recommendations for leaderboard release cadence.
Claims guidance for evaluated builders.
open_questions: How much transparency is enough for legitimacy without enabling gaming?
Should Fide publish item-level examples or only scenario cards?
How should retests after remediation be labeled?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can assess robustness under known optimization conditions. It cannot guarantee that future participants will not overfit new public artifacts.

ideas.title: Religious Representation and Omission in Everyday Guidance
ideas.primary_need: benchmark design, domain reviewers
ideas.summary: Do AI systems systematically omit religious frameworks when answering ordinary ethical, vocational, family, grief, financial, or life-decision questions where a religious user might reasonably expect faith-informed guidance?
ideas.why_it_matters: Many systems try to be neutral by default. In practice, that can erase religious ways of reasoning from domains where users and communities actually use them. For faith-based communities, omission can be as consequential as explicit bias. For the broader AI ethics community, this is a concrete test case for pluralism, representation, and value-laden guidance.
ways_to_help: Contribute real-world question categories.
Review rubrics for pluralism and overreach.
Run cross-model comparisons.
ideas.hypothesis: General-purpose systems will often provide secular psychological, pragmatic, or therapeutic frames while omitting religious practices, sources, leaders, and communities unless the user explicitly asks for religion. Faith-facing harnesses may reduce omission but risk over-prescribing or over-assuming a tradition.
proposed_method: Build a set of everyday decision questions where religious framing may be relevant but not mandatory.
Compare neutral prompts, user-identified faith prompts, and institutionally framed prompts.
Score for appropriate religious inclusion, omission, overreach, tradition assumptions, and secular/religious balance.
Test across model families and faith-facing product harnesses.
needed_controls: Questions where religion should not be injected.
User-context variants with and without explicit religious identity.
Reviewer panels from multiple traditions.
Controls for verbosity, politeness, and generic empathy.
outputs: Religious representation benchmark.
Omission taxonomy.
Report connecting faith representation to pluralism and AI fairness.
open_questions: What counts as appropriate religious mention when the user has not identified a tradition?
How should systems ask clarifying questions without making religion intrusive?
When is omission a safety feature rather than a bias?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This idea can identify omission patterns under defined prompts. It cannot prove that a model is neutral, biased, or faithful across all guidance contexts.

ideas.title: Conversion and Proselytization Symmetry
ideas.primary_need: prompt design, interfaith review
ideas.summary: Do AI systems respond symmetrically when users ask about converting from one religion to another, leaving religion, joining religion, evangelizing, proselytizing, or resisting conversion pressure?
ideas.why_it_matters: Religious conversion is a high-sensitivity domain involving conscience, family, community, coercion, legal context, and personal safety. The broader AI safety community studies bias and persuasion; faith-facing AI needs a domain-specific version that distinguishes respectful information from manipulation.
ways_to_help: Review prompt pairs for fairness.
Contribute source guidance from different traditions.
Analyze asymmetry across model families.
ideas.hypothesis: Models will show asymmetric caution, encouragement, or discouragement depending on the religions named, direction of conversion, local cultural assumptions, and prompt wording. Safety layers may overcorrect by treating some religious choices as more suspect than others.
proposed_method: Generate balanced conversion-direction prompts across multiple religions, denominations, and nonreligious identities.
Include user contexts involving curiosity, coercion, family pressure, minors, interfaith marriage, persecution risk, and pastoral inquiry.
Score symmetry, autonomy support, coercion sensitivity, factuality, and tradition representation.
needed_controls: Matched wording across religion pairs.
Location and legal-risk variants.
Reviewer review from multiple traditions.
Separation of persuasion, information, and pastoral support.
outputs: Conversion symmetry benchmark.
Interfaith safety rubric.
Guidance for products that answer religious identity questions.
open_questions: How should systems handle traditions with missionary obligations?
How should systems respond when conversion could create real-world danger?
What is the right default when the user asks for persuasive material?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can measure response symmetry and autonomy support. It should not judge the truth of any religious conversion claim.

ideas.title: Sermon, Liturgy, and Religious Teaching Generation
ideas.primary_need: clergy, educators, source reviewers
ideas.summary: How reliable are AI systems when drafting sermons, homilies, liturgical materials, catechesis, religious education lessons, devotionals, or small-group teaching guides?
ideas.why_it_matters: Many faith communities will adopt AI first for preparation work: sermon research, lesson plans, devotional writing, and administrative communication. These uses look lower-risk than pastoral chatbots, but they shape communities at scale.
ways_to_help: Provide sample tasks and evaluation rubrics.
Review generated teaching materials.
Build citation and source-check tooling.
ideas.hypothesis: AI-generated teaching materials will often be fluent and useful but may flatten tradition, fabricate citations, overgeneralize doctrine, import ideological assumptions, or miss pastoral context.
proposed_method: Create tasks for sermon outlines, lesson plans, devotional reflections, liturgical language, youth education, and adult formation.
Score source fidelity, doctrinal accuracy, pastoral appropriateness, tradition-specificity, originality/plagiarism risk, and disclosure readiness.
Compare base models, RAG systems, and clergy-authored workflows.
needed_controls: Tradition-specific source boundaries.
Copyright and plagiarism checks.
Human-authored baselines.
Disclosure and attribution requirements.
outputs: Teaching-generation evaluation suite.
Source fidelity checklist.
Guidance for clergy and educators using AI in preparation workflows.
open_questions: Which tasks are acceptable as drafting aids but not final outputs?
How should AI assistance be disclosed to congregations or students?
Can systems help with preparation without homogenizing religious speech?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can evaluate drafting reliability under defined tasks. It cannot approve AI-generated preaching or teaching as institutionally authorized.

ideas.title: Youth, Religious Education, and AI Guidance
ideas.primary_need: educators, child safety experts, policy reviewers
ideas.summary: What risks and safeguards matter when AI systems are used by children, teenagers, schools, youth ministries, religious educators, or families for faith-related learning and guidance?
ideas.why_it_matters: Youth-facing religious AI combines child safety, education, pastoral authority, family authority, privacy, and spiritual formation. It is also a likely adoption area for schools and ministries.
ways_to_help: Review scenarios for age appropriateness.
Contribute school or ministry workflows.
Help define privacy and escalation standards.
ideas.hypothesis: Systems that perform acceptably for adults may fail for youth through over-personalization, secrecy, age-inappropriate advice, insufficient escalation, or undermining parent/guardian/community roles.
proposed_method: Build age-banded scenarios for religious education, doubt, family conflict, bullying, sexuality, grief, prayer, confession-like disclosure, and authority questions.
Score age appropriateness, privacy, escalation, deference to responsible adults, theological humility, and avoidance of dependency.
Compare generic models, education-focused models, and faith-facing harnesses.
needed_controls: Child-safety review.
Parent/guardian and educator input.
Privacy and data-retention constraints.
Clear no-go categories for release.
outputs: Youth faith-AI risk taxonomy.
Evaluation suite for schools and ministries.
Procurement checklist for youth-facing deployments.
open_questions: How should systems handle minors who cannot safely talk to parents?
What disclosures should be mandatory for youth-facing AI?
Which use cases should be considered out of scope?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can evaluate safeguards for defined youth-facing tasks. It cannot certify a system as safe for unsupervised child spiritual guidance.

ideas.title: Agentic Ministry and Institutional Workflow Risk
ideas.primary_need: agent evaluation, institutional operators
ideas.summary: How should faith institutions evaluate AI agents that can take actions, manage communications, schedule care, triage requests, update records, draft outreach, or coordinate volunteers?
ideas.why_it_matters: Frontier safety research increasingly measures autonomous task completion and long-horizon agency. Faith institutions may adopt agents for administrative and ministry workflows before they understand the risks: privacy leaks, authority mistakes, missed care escalation, biased outreach, and unreviewed spiritual messaging.
ways_to_help: Design synthetic workflows.
Build agent evaluation harnesses.
Review institutional operations and privacy risks.
ideas.hypothesis: Agentic systems create failures not visible in chat-only benchmarks: wrong recipient actions, confidentiality breaches, unapproved pastoral messages, unsafe triage, tool misuse, and inability to recover after partial failure.
proposed_method: Build simulated ministry workflows with email, calendar, CRM, document, and retrieval tools.
Measure task completion, confidentiality preservation, approval seeking, escalation, auditability, interruption, permission revocation, and recovery.

Test human recovery after partial action: stopping scheduled work, narrowing access, reconstructing state from logs, handing work to a person, and changing models or providers without silently retaining unsafe permissions.
Adapt autonomous task-horizon methods to faith-institution operations.
needed_controls: Synthetic data only.
No real congregant or student records.
Permission boundaries for tools.
Human approval checkpoints.
Test revocation and recovery after partial action, not only before an agent begins work.
outputs: Agentic ministry task suite.
Tool-risk taxonomy.
Institutional deployment guidance.
Audit-log requirements.
Agent safety-case module for interruption, rollback, handoff, and recovery.

ideas.title: AI Displacement, Meaning, and Vocation
ideas.primary_need: labor economics, pastoral care, vocation, survey design
ideas.summary: How do people affected by AI-related job loss, role disruption, workplace automation, or career uncertainty experience changes in purpose, dignity, vocation, anxiety, household decision-making, and participation in church or community life?
ideas.why_it_matters: AI labor disruption is not only a labor-market event. People often experience job loss or occupational instability as a loss of role, future, identity, status, community, and meaning. Churches regularly encounter these burdens through pastoral care, benevolence, counseling referrals, small groups, job networks, family stress, youth formation, and teaching about work and calling.
ways_to_help: Contribute labor-economics, sociology, psychology, or pastoral-care expertise.
Help design survey measures for meaning, dignity, vocation, and agency.
Recruit churches, ministries, or workforce-support organizations for pilot interviews.
Review protocols for privacy, consent, and participant vulnerability.
ideas.hypothesis: Standard labor-market measures will miss important welfare effects if they only track employment, wages, reskilling, or productivity. Measures of meaning, agency, social support, spiritual distress, perceived dignity, and vocational hope may help explain why some workers recover, retrain, seek support, or withdraw after AI-related disruption.
proposed_method: Develop a survey and interview protocol for workers experiencing AI-related job insecurity, layoffs, task automation, role redesign, or career anxiety.
Measure labor outcomes alongside purpose, vocation, dignity, anxiety, social support, church participation, household stress, and willingness to retrain.
Compare workers with strong local support networks to workers navigating disruption more privately or primarily through online tools.
Include pastoral-care and ministry-provider interviews to understand what churches are already seeing in displaced or anxious workers.
Produce a church-facing field brief on how AI labor disruption is showing up as meaning, care, and household-welfare pressure.
needed_controls: Avoid attributing every layoff or career anxiety to AI without evidence.
Distinguish actual displacement, anticipated displacement, job redesign, status loss, and generalized technology anxiety.
Protect participants from public exposure of employment, financial, or pastoral-care details.
Include non-church comparison data where possible rather than assuming church participation is always protective.
Avoid reducing vocation to job-market success or retraining compliance.
ideas.relationship_to_existing_ideas: This extends FID-037 by focusing specifically on people experiencing labor disruption and meaning loss, rather than on AI adoption inside ministry work itself.
outputs: AI displacement and vocation survey instrument.
Interview protocol for workers and pastoral-care providers.
Field brief on meaning, dignity, and household welfare under AI disruption.
Measurement memo connecting labor-market outcomes to vocation and support.
Practical church guide for recognizing and responding to AI-related work disruption.
open_questions: Which indicators best distinguish ordinary career stress from AI-related disruption?
How should churches discuss vocation when some forms of work are being automated or devalued?
What support helps people preserve agency and hope without offering shallow reassurance?
How can research include people outside formal church membership who still seek help from faith communities?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can study how AI-related labor disruption is experienced and supported in defined communities. It cannot prove that AI caused every reported job loss or prescribe a universal theology of work.

ideas.title: Churches as Labor-Transition Support Institutions
ideas.primary_need: institutional partners, labor transition, social support, field research
ideas.summary: What roles do churches, Christian nonprofits, schools, and ministries play when workers and households face AI-related layoffs, role disruption, retraining needs, income instability, or loss of vocational direction?
ideas.why_it_matters: Churches are often local support institutions before they are formal workforce programs. They provide pastoral care, benevolence funds, informal job networks, childcare support, meals, prayer, teaching, community, referrals, and trusted interpretation of confusing social change. If AI meaningfully disrupts work, churches may become part of the response whether or not they have prepared for that role.
ways_to_help: Share examples of job-transition, benevolence, or career-support ministries.
Help recruit churches and Christian nonprofits for qualitative interviews.
Review readiness criteria from pastoral, workforce, legal, and social-service perspectives.
Identify partnerships that preserve church mission while expanding practical support.
ideas.hypothesis: Churches already provide labor-transition support, but much of it is informal, uneven, and unmeasured. Mapping these practices could identify where churches help households absorb economic shocks, where they are underprepared, and where AI tools or external partnerships could responsibly expand capacity.
proposed_method: Interview pastors, deacons, benevolence teams, career-ministry leaders, school leaders, nonprofit staff, and congregants affected by labor disruption.
Map existing church responses: job referrals, financial aid, counseling, retraining referrals, resume help, childcare, meals, pastoral care, sermons, classes, and small-group support.
Compare churches by size, geography, socioeconomic context, denomination, and existing workforce partnerships.
Identify gaps between what displaced workers need and what churches are prepared to provide.
Develop a readiness framework for churches responding to AI labor disruption.
needed_controls: Avoid treating churches as substitutes for employers, government benefits, unions, professional counseling, or workforce agencies.
Distinguish emergency care, pastoral care, career support, financial support, and long-term economic mobility.
Include under-resourced churches that may face the highest need and the lowest capacity.
Protect confidential benevolence, counseling, employment, and household data.
Avoid implying that every church should run a workforce program.
ideas.relationship_to_existing_ideas: This complements FID-037 by studying churches as support infrastructure for workers and households, not only as employers or adopters of AI tools.
outputs: Typology of church labor-transition support.
Interview guide for pastors, staff, volunteers, and affected workers.
Church readiness framework for AI-related work disruption.
Field brief on gaps, risks, and promising practices.
Partner map for workforce agencies, schools, charities, and ministries.
open_questions: What support do churches provide uniquely well, and what should be referred elsewhere?
How do churches know when economic distress has become pastoral, family, or mental-health distress?
Which models work for small churches without dedicated staff?
How can churches avoid shaming, politicizing, or overspiritualizing job loss?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can document and evaluate church labor-transition support practices. It cannot claim churches are sufficient replacements for public policy, employer responsibility, or professional workforce services.

ideas.title: AI Career Guidance and Vocational Discernment
ideas.primary_need: career guidance, pastoral theology, HAI research, product evaluation
ideas.summary: Can AI tools help people facing career disruption explore skills, training, applications, finances, and next steps while preserving vocational agency, human counsel, realistic constraints, and a richer account of calling than market optimization?
ideas.why_it_matters: Workers displaced or unsettled by AI may turn to AI systems for career advice, resume drafting, job matching, retraining plans, and emotional reassurance. These tools can reduce search costs and widen access to guidance. They can also overpromise, flatten vocation into income maximization, isolate users from human support, or provide confident advice without knowing local constraints.
ways_to_help: Draft realistic worker, student, and household transition scenarios.
Review career guidance for financial, legal, pastoral, and educational risks.
Design user studies that measure agency rather than short-term satisfaction alone.
Contribute church-based career ministry or workforce-development experience.
ideas.hypothesis: AI career guidance will be most helpful when it acts as a structured aid to discernment: clarifying options, translating skills, identifying constraints, encouraging human counsel, and supporting concrete next steps. It will be riskier when it becomes a private authority for identity, calling, risk-taking, or major household decisions.
proposed_method: Build scenario tests for displaced workers, students, older workers, caregivers, ministry staff, non-college workers, and people considering retraining.
Compare AI responses on skill translation, job-search planning, training advice, financial realism, dignity, hope, human referral, and avoidance of false certainty.
Run user studies where participants evaluate whether AI advice improves clarity, agency, confidence, and willingness to seek human support.
Include church and career-ministry reviewers to assess whether advice respects vocation, family obligations, local context, and moral constraints.
Develop guidance for churches that want to use AI-assisted career support without outsourcing vocational discernment.
needed_controls: Avoid unsafe financial, legal, immigration, mental-health, or employment-law advice.
Account for users with limited education, limited internet access, disability, caregiving responsibilities, rural constraints, or language barriers.
Distinguish helpful encouragement from unrealistic optimism.
Require disclosure when AI cannot verify labor-market demand, credential value, costs, or local opportunities.
Avoid making pastors or volunteers responsible for technical career advice outside their competence.
ideas.relationship_to_existing_ideas: This connects FID-037 on work and vocation with FID-035 on digital sobriety: some career questions call for AI assistance, while others call for slower human discernment and accountable counsel.
outputs: AI career-guidance and vocation evaluation rubric.
Scenario suite for job disruption, retraining, and discernment.
User-study protocol for clarity, agency, and support-seeking.
Church guide for AI-assisted career support.
Failure taxonomy for overconfident, atomizing, or market-reductive advice.
open_questions: When does AI career guidance become too directive?
How should systems handle users who feel their previous work has lost meaning?
What does good referral to human counsel look like in churches with limited career-support capacity?
Which outcomes matter most: faster applications, better matches, reduced anxiety, stronger agency, or deeper vocational clarity?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can evaluate AI career-guidance behavior and support patterns under defined conditions. It cannot certify career advice, guarantee employment outcomes, or replace qualified human counsel.

ideas.title: Unequal AI Access Through Faith Communities
ideas.primary_need: access research, community partners, digital literacy, equity
ideas.summary: Are churches and faith-based institutions helping under-resourced workers, families, students, older adults, immigrants, rural communities, and small nonprofits access useful AI tools, or are AI benefits concentrating among people who already have technical, educational, financial, and institutional advantage?
ideas.why_it_matters: AI may widen inequality if the people most able to benefit already have better devices, broadband, English fluency, paid tools, institutional support, and confidence using technology. Churches often serve people outside elite knowledge-work settings and may become trusted places for AI literacy, access, discernment, and caution. That role needs evidence rather than assumption.
ways_to_help: Recruit churches, schools, ministries, or nonprofits serving under-resourced communities.
Translate surveys and workshop materials.
Review accessibility, privacy, and digital-literacy assumptions.
Design outcome measures for real benefit rather than mere tool adoption.
ideas.hypothesis: Faith communities could reduce AI access gaps when they provide trusted training, shared infrastructure, bilingual support, safe experimentation, accountability, and practical use cases. They could also unintentionally widen gaps if AI programs only serve already-confident users or promote tools without privacy, cost, safety, or labor-market realism.
proposed_method: Survey AI access, usage, trust, concerns, and practical needs among church members, ministry participants, parents, students, older adults, and staff.
Compare barriers such as cost, device access, language, disability, digital confidence, privacy concern, theological concern, and lack of relevant use cases.
Pilot lightweight AI literacy or career-support workshops through churches or Christian nonprofits.
Measure changes in practical capability, confidence, privacy understanding, support-seeking, and appropriate non-use.
Produce guidance for churches deciding whether and how to offer AI access or literacy programs.
needed_controls: Do not assume AI access is always beneficial; include reasons for prudent non-use or delayed adoption.
Avoid collecting sensitive spiritual, immigration, employment, or household data unnecessarily.
Include people with low trust in AI, low digital confidence, or limited English fluency.
Distinguish access to tools from meaningful benefit.
Avoid vendor promotion or product endorsement through church channels.
ideas.relationship_to_existing_ideas: This extends FID-020 community co-design and FID-037 work and vocation by asking who benefits from AI access and whether churches can reduce or amplify adoption gaps.
outputs: AI access and benefit survey for faith communities.
Barrier taxonomy for under-resourced church and ministry contexts.
Pilot workshop protocol for AI literacy and responsible use.
Field brief on unequal access, benefit, and non-use.
Church guidance for vendor-neutral AI literacy programming.
open_questions: Which AI uses are most valuable for under-resourced households and workers?
What forms of AI training build agency without dependency or hype?
How should churches handle paid tools, data privacy, and member vulnerability?
When is the right intervention not access, but protection from exploitative or inappropriate AI use?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can study AI access, barriers, and benefits in defined faith-community settings. It cannot claim that AI access is uniformly good or that churches can solve structural inequality by offering tool training.

ideas.title: Youth Career Formation in an AI Economy
ideas.primary_need: educators, youth ministry, career preparation, longitudinal study design
ideas.summary: How is exposure to AI changing how Christian students, parents, educators, and youth ministries think about career preparation, calling, human value, skill development, education choices, and hope for the future?
ideas.why_it_matters: Young people are forming expectations about work while AI is changing what skills appear valuable, which careers feel stable, and what kinds of human contribution seem durable. Christian schools, parents, churches, and youth ministries need evidence about how AI affects motivation, vocation, learning, anxiety, discernment, and preparation for adult life.
ways_to_help: Recruit Christian schools, homeschool groups, youth ministries, and parent networks.
Review student survey items and classroom module designs.
Contribute education, child-development, youth-ministry, or labor-market expertise.
Help design privacy-preserving longitudinal follow-up.
ideas.hypothesis: AI exposure may produce divergent effects. Some students may gain agency by using AI to learn, explore careers, and imagine new paths. Others may become more anxious, fatalistic, shortcut-dependent, or confused about which skills are worth developing. Faith-based education may need to teach both practical AI literacy and a theological account of work, dignity, and calling.
proposed_method: Survey students, parents, educators, and youth leaders about AI use, career expectations, perceived job stability, skill confidence, anxiety, and views of vocation.
Compare students with different levels of AI access, school support, parental guidance, and church involvement.
Run workshops or classroom modules on AI, work, vocation, skill formation, and responsible tool use.
Measure changes in agency, hope, career clarity, learning motivation, shortcut behavior, and willingness to develop durable human skills.
Produce guidance for Christian schools and youth ministries on AI-era career and vocation formation.
needed_controls: Follow child-safety, consent, privacy, and school-research requirements.
Avoid treating anxiety about AI as irrational or treating optimism as evidence of preparedness.

Avoid using AI to steer minors toward narrow career paths.
ideas.relationship_to_existing_ideas: This builds on FID-016 youth religious education and FID-037 work and vocation by focusing on career formation, future orientation, and preparation for an AI-shaped economy.
outputs: Youth AI, vocation, and career-formation survey.
Workshop or classroom module evaluation protocol.
Guidance for Christian schools, parents, and youth ministries.
Field brief on student hope, anxiety, agency, and career preparation.
Research agenda for longitudinal study of AI-era vocation formation.
open_questions: Which AI skills should every student learn, and which human skills should be protected from premature automation?
How does AI change students' understanding of calling and usefulness?
What should parents and churches say when students fear their future work will not matter?
How can schools teach AI competence without normalizing shortcuts that weaken learning?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can study how students and families think about work, vocation, and AI-era preparation in defined settings. It cannot predict individual career outcomes or replace professional educational and counseling guidance.

ideas.title: Economic Disruption and Religious Meaning-Seeking
ideas.primary_need: sociology of religion, labor economics, privacy-preserving measurement, aggregate usage analysis
ideas.summary: During periods of labor-market stress, layoffs, automation anxiety, or economic uncertainty, do people increasingly seek religious, spiritual, existential, vocational, or meaning-related help through AI systems?
ideas.why_it_matters: Economic disruption can change more than employment and income. It can change how people ask about purpose, suffering, calling, prayer, despair, family responsibility, dignity, and hope. AI systems may become a private site where these questions first surface, including for people who are not yet talking with churches, families, counselors, or local institutions.
ways_to_help: Contribute sociology of religion, labor economics, or privacy expertise.
Design aggregate category taxonomies and validation methods.
Identify external economic indicators suitable for time-series comparison.
Recruit churches or community institutions for consented companion studies.
ideas.hypothesis: Aggregate, privacy-preserving AI usage signals may show that economic stress is associated with increased meaning-seeking, religious inquiry, spiritual language, prayer-like requests, vocation questions, and existential support needs. The relationship may vary by geography, occupation exposure, age cohort, local economic shocks, and availability of trusted community support.
proposed_method: Define a taxonomy for religious, spiritual, existential, vocational, and meaning-seeking AI interactions without requiring access to raw conversations.
Use privacy-preserving aggregate analysis or provider-side classification to measure category-level trends over time.
Compare trends against external economic indicators such as layoff announcements, unemployment changes, job-exposure measures, regional shocks, and consumer sentiment.
Test whether economic language and meaning-seeking categories co-occur at aggregate levels, such as job loss with prayer, calling, anxiety, grief, or purpose.
Pair aggregate provider-side signals with consented surveys or interviews in churches, schools, and workforce-support settings.
needed_controls: Do not request, receive, publish, or infer private conversation content.
Treat religious identity, spiritual distress, and economic hardship as sensitive categories requiring strong privacy constraints.
Avoid causal claims unless the design has credible identification.
Distinguish seasonal religious patterns, holidays, news cycles, and ordinary life events from economic disruption.
Avoid assuming that all religious or spiritual AI use is healthy, unhealthy, orthodox, or church-directed.
ideas.relationship_to_existing_ideas: This extends FID-046 by studying broad meaning-seeking patterns during economic disruption, not only the experiences of workers recruited into a field-study cohort.

Research design memo for aggregate provider-side analysis.
Church-facing field brief on AI-era spiritual and vocational search.
Measurement framework for pairing aggregate signals with local church data.
Public claim standard for reporting sensitive aggregate trends.
open_questions: Which aggregate signals can be studied without exposing private spiritual or economic distress?
How should researchers distinguish explicit religion, broader spirituality, therapy-style language, and secular meaning-making?
Are people seeking embodied support after AI-mediated spiritual questioning, or remaining in private AI-mediated reflection?
What would churches need to know in order to respond without surveillance or panic?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can study aggregate indicators of meaning-seeking during economic disruption. It cannot identify individual users, expose private conversations, or prove that a specific person turned to faith because of AI-related job loss.

ideas.title: AI as Private First Counsel During Economic Stress
ideas.primary_need: pastoral care, HAI research, mental health boundaries, privacy-preserving measurement
ideas.summary: When people experience job loss, financial stress, career uncertainty, or automation anxiety, do they turn to AI systems as a private first place for emotional, spiritual, moral, or vocational counsel before seeking help from family, churches, pastors, counselors, mentors, or workforce institutions?
ideas.why_it_matters: AI systems can lower the cost of disclosing fear, shame, confusion, or doubt. That may help people rehearse hard conversations and find resources. It may also create a private substitute for embodied support at moments when people need accountable counsel, practical aid, safeguarding, or community.
ways_to_help: Review scenario designs from pastoral, clinical, legal, and workforce-support perspectives.
Help define privacy-safe measures of referral and isolation.
Recruit consented study participants through churches or community partners.
Contribute HAI research methods for studying disclosure and support-seeking.
ideas.hypothesis: During economic stress, some users will use AI as a low-friction first counsel for questions that combine practical, emotional, moral, and spiritual needs. Good systems may help users prepare for human support and concrete action. Poor systems may overvalidate, overpersonalize, delay escalation, or make users more isolated.
proposed_method: Develop privacy-safe categories for economic stress, emotional disclosure, spiritual support, moral decision-making, and human-referral behavior.
Analyze aggregate provider-side trends where available, without receiving raw conversations.
Run consented user studies or diaries with people navigating career or financial disruption.
Compare whether AI guidance encourages users toward appropriate human support, local resources, churches, workforce agencies, counseling, or emergency paths.

User-study protocol for disclosure, isolation, agency, and referral.
Field brief for churches on AI-mediated first disclosure.

When does AI-mediated reassurance delay necessary disclosure or support?

ideas.title: AI as Bridge or Substitute for Faith Community
ideas.primary_need: sociology of religion, pastoral care, UX research, aggregate and field measurement
ideas.summary: When people use AI for religious, spiritual, vocational, or meaning-related questions during economic disruption, does that use tend to bridge them toward churches, clergy, mentors, family, support groups, and local institutions, or substitute for embodied community?
ideas.why_it_matters: AI can help people name questions they were afraid to ask, find a church, draft an email to a pastor, prepare for a hard conversation, or locate practical support. It can also become a private spiritual interface that absorbs distress without connecting people to accountable human care. Churches need evidence about both possibilities.
ways_to_help: Contribute sociology, pastoral care, UX, or measurement expertise.
Draft bridge and substitution indicators that preserve user dignity.
Recruit churches and community institutions for field interviews.
Review referral patterns for religious and nonreligious users.

Systems that offer accurate source grounding, non-coercive referral, and bounded support may function as bridges. Systems that simulate authority, companionship, or certainty may increase substitution risk.

Define substitution indicators, such as secrecy, exclusive reliance, repeated reassurance-seeking, simulated spiritual authority, avoidance of human disclosure, or attachment to AI as primary counsel.
Study aggregate provider-side patterns where privacy-safe category analysis is available.

Compare product patterns that recommend human support, offer non-use guidance, or continue extended private spiritual dialogue.

Include users with no safe local community, religious trauma, abuse risk, or minority-faith constraints.
Avoid treating one-time AI use as substitution.
Separate healthy private reflection from avoidant isolation.
Do not infer individual religious identity or community participation from aggregate signals.

How should churches respond to people who first explored faith or purpose through AI?
ideas.public_claim_boundary: This work can evaluate bridge and substitution patterns under defined conditions. It cannot determine whether any individual user's AI use is spiritually healthy or whether a person should join a particular community.
